title: SQL for people who write reports
summary: Write the queries behind a weekly report without waiting on the data team. Ends with a report you build from a real extract.
tagline: Stop logging a ticket every time you need a number.
description: Most reporting jobs stall in the same place. The numbers live in a database, the database is behind a request form, and the answer arrives three days after the meeting. This course takes that dependency away for the queries you run most weeks.

You work in a copy of a real sales and support extract from the first module onwards. Every concept is introduced because the report you are building needs it, so nothing is taught in the abstract and nothing is taught twice.
outcomes: Read a database schema and find the table you actually need
Filter, sort and group a result set without exporting it to a spreadsheet first
Join tables correctly, and recognise the join that silently duplicated your rows
Aggregate by week, month and quarter for a report that refreshes itself
Write a query someone else can read and hand over six months later
Sanity-check a number before you put it in front of a manager

title: Spreadsheets that survive an audit
summary: Build workbooks someone else can check. Covers structure, formulas that do not break, and the habits auditors look for.
tagline: The workbook is only finished when somebody else can check it.
description: A spreadsheet that only its author can follow is a liability, and it usually becomes one at the worst possible moment. This course is about the difference between a file that works and a file that holds up when a reviewer, an auditor or your replacement opens it.

You rebuild a real budget workbook that failed a review, fixing it structurally rather than patching the numbers. The habits are small: separate inputs from calculations, name what you reference, leave a trail. Together they are what an auditor is actually looking for.
outcomes: Lay out a workbook so inputs, calculations and outputs never mix
Write formulas that do not break when a row is inserted
Replace fragile lookups with references that explain themselves
Build in checks that fail loudly instead of quietly
Document assumptions where the reviewer will actually read them
Hand a workbook over without a thirty-minute explanation

title: React for the first real project
summary: Go from tutorials to shipping. Components, state, routing and the parts of a codebase nobody explains until you are already in one.
tagline: The gap between finishing a tutorial and being useful on a team.
description: Tutorials end where real work starts. You can build a counter, and then you open a repository with forty components, a router, a design system and a code review waiting, and none of it looks like the tutorial.

This course builds one application across fourteen hours, the way a team would: components first, then state, then routing, then the unglamorous parts — loading states, errors, empty states, accessibility and the review that sends it back. You finish with a project worth linking to, and with the vocabulary to follow a conversation about someone else's code.
outcomes: Break an interface into components that stay reusable
Choose between local state, lifted state and context, and justify it
Fetch data with loading, error and empty states handled from the start
Add routing, including nested routes and URL parameters
Write accessible markup and keyboard-usable interactions by default
Read an unfamiliar codebase and find where a change belongs
Take review feedback and rework code without starting over

title: Running a delivery without chaos
summary: Scope, estimates and the stakeholder conversation that keeps changing. Practical delivery for people who inherited the job.
tagline: For the person who was handed the project, not trained for it.
description: Most delivery managers were something else first. The plan is inherited, the scope moves weekly, and the certification courses are written for a project that behaves.

This course covers the three things that actually decide whether a delivery lands: what is in scope, what it will realistically take, and how you hold a conversation with a stakeholder who wants both dates. You run a delivery that goes wrong on purpose, and practise the recovery.
outcomes: Write a scope statement that makes exclusions explicit
Produce a range estimate you can defend, and explain the range
Spot scope creep in the week it starts rather than at the deadline
Run a status conversation that surfaces bad news early
Renegotiate a date without losing credibility
Close a delivery so the next one starts from something
